findings.claim: Your exam will always ask you to show your working — so understanding the formula, substituting correctly, and writing the unit are all part of a full-marks response.
findings.truth: The external assessment includes objective, short and extended responses; it does not require working on every question.

findings.claim: Examiners award method marks for each step, so a correct method still gains marks after an arithmetic error.
findings.truth: Marks are awarded under the question's mark scheme. The specification does not guarantee method marks for every calculation step.

findings.claim: Every one of these skills is tested in your exam.
findings.truth: Each paper assesses content from every topic area, while individual content is assessed over the lifespan of the specification; not every skill is guaranteed in every paper.

findings.claim: Real length always equals drawing length multiplied by the scale denominator, and drawing length always equals real length divided by the denominator.
findings.truth: For a scale written a:b, real length = drawing length × b ÷ a and drawing length = real length × a ÷ b. The original shortcut fails for enlargement scales such as 2:1.
findings.evidence: recomputation; spec 3.4.1 includes enlargement and reduction

findings.claim: The area formulae are not given on the paper.
findings.truth: The specification's assessment section does not state whether a formula sheet is supplied. Confirm this against current assessment material before retaining or removing the assertion.

findings.claim: With equal class widths, frequency can be read directly from a histogram bar's height.
findings.truth: A histogram represents frequency by bar area. Equal widths make height proportional to frequency, but whether height itself is a frequency depends on the vertical-axis label and scale.

findings.claim: Every orthographic drawing has three standard views.
findings.truth: An orthographic drawing can use up to six primary views, although three views are usually enough.
findings.evidence: fetched Wikipedia, Multiview orthographic projection, lines 132-134

findings.claim: Third-angle projection is the standard used in the United Kingdom.
findings.truth: Keep third-angle layout because the specification explicitly requires it. Remove the UK-standard claims: BS 8888 permits labelled, first-angle and third-angle arrangements, and first-angle has traditionally been common in the UK. This correction also appears in conclusion_html, practice_questions and flashcard_questions, so it needs a coordinated decision.
findings.evidence: spec 3.4.2; fetched Wikipedia, Multiview orthographic projection, lines 260-264 and 308

findings.claim: Isometric projection preserves true lengths along all three axes.
findings.truth: In strict technical usage, an isometric projection foreshortens all axes equally (about 80%); an isometric drawing uses true lengths. The specification asks for isometric views, so either use the school-convention term consistently or teach the distinction. The wording recurs in content, conclusion and glossary.
findings.evidence: spec 3.4.2; fetched Wikipedia, Isometric projection, lines 143-155

summary: Seven verified, surgical corrections are supplied. One unsupported assessment assertion is noted, and two repeated drawing-convention issues require coordinated editorial choices.
